title: Supplemental Comments of Transmission Access Policy Study Group on FERC's proposed Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking under RM26-4.

documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                 BEFORE THE
                   FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Interconnection of Large Loads to the                     Docket No. RM26-4-000
    Interstate Transmission System


                      SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF
                 TRANSMISSION ACCESS POLICY STUDY GROUP


        The Transmission Access Policy Study Group (“TAPS”), an association of

transmission-dependent utilities (“TDUs”) in thirty-nine states promoting open and non-

discriminatory transmission access, respectfully submits these supplemental comments

on the Secretary of Energy’s proposed Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

(“ANOPR”) 1 under consideration by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (the

“Commission”). While TAPS’s opening comments addressed a broad range of important

issues raised in the ANOPR, 2 these Supplemental Comments focus on two critical issues

raised in recent supplemental comments.

        First, we address the filing submitted by the National Association of Regulatory

Commissioners (“NARUC”), 3 which argues that no Commission action is needed in light

of recent actions taken by some (but not all) states regarding some (but not all) issues

related to large load interconnections. While TAPS agrees that it is important that the

Commission respect jurisdictional boundaries, action by this Commission is required to




1
 Secretary of Energy, Ensuring the Timely and Orderly Interconnection of Large Loads, Advanced Notice
of Proposed Rulemaking (released Oct. 23, 2023), eLibrary No. 20251027-4001 (“ANOPR”).
2
  Comments of Transmission Access Policy Study Group (Nov. 21, 2025), eLibrary No. 20251121-5346
(“TAPS Comments” or “TAPS opening comments”).
3
  Supplemental Comments of National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners (Apr. 13, 2026),
eLibrary No. 20260413-5278 (“NARUC Supplemental Comments”).
                                                -2-


address the clear and direct impact that large load 4 interconnections have on transmission

rates within the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction. The Commission is statutorily

obligated to ensure just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory transmission rates;

only the Commission can protect other wholesale transmission customers from the risks

of significant large load-driven cost shifting and stranded costs that would otherwise

occur through Commission-jurisdictional rates.

        Second, we address the Supplemental Comments and attached whitepaper

submitted by WIRES, 5 which claim that the Commission’s “and” pricing policy must

fully exempt large loads from ongoing transmission charges if the Commission initially

holds them responsible for the costs of network upgrades they cause. That claim—which

the WIRES whitepaper admits fails to consider the significant stranded cost risk posed by

large loads—is wrong. The Commission is free to modify its decades-old “and” pricing

policy to ensure just and reasonable transmission rates in light of the new and unique

challenges posed by large load interconnections. Alternatively, a specially designed

mechanism that permits large loads to receive credits to offset their upfront network

upgrade cost responsibility, provided that they sustain over time the level of transmission

service demand for which they were planned, can help protect other customers while

avoiding concerns about “and” pricing.




4
  In our opening comments, TAPS used the term “Qualifying Large Loads” to cover a large, individual
retail customer seeking to interconnect directly to the transmission system and meeting other to-be-
determined qualifications. As the supplemental comments to which we are responding here do not use that
terminology, our supplemental comments use “large loads” to refer to such loads to avoid confusion.
5
 Supplemental Comments of WIRES (Mar. 30, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260330-5308 (“WIRES
Supplemental Comments”).
                                              -3-


                              SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS

I.        COMMISSION ACTION IS NEEDED BECAUSE ONLY THIS
          COMMISSION CAN ENSURE JUST, REASONABLE, AND NOT
          UNDULY DISCRIMINATORY TRANSMISSION RATES.

          NARUC claims that “no action in the ANOPR is necessary to enable state

commission[s] to cost-allocate transmission between end-use customers,” and that

therefore there is “no regulatory gap” that requires Commission action.6 While TAPS

agrees that the Commission should not intrude on matters subject to state and local

jurisdiction, 7 state authority over retail matters in no way eliminates the need for the

Commission to take decisive action on the important issues raised in the ANOPR that fall

squarely within the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction.

          As NARUC notes, state regulators have authority to “determine the cost

allocation of transmission costs among retail ratepayers.” 8 But that authority does not

extend to interstate transmission rates. State regulators thus cannot address what should

be included in the wholesale transmission revenue requirement or the allocation of

transmission costs among wholesale transmission customers. That authority belongs

solely to this Commission.

          There is no question that the huge increase in new and upgraded transmission

facilities needed to serve large load interconnections have a direct and significant impact

on Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates. For instance, some Commission-

jurisdictional transmission costs are allocated among Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”)

based on their relative load ratio shares in the transmission zone, which may span


6
    NARUC Supplemental Comments at 6.
7
    TAPS Comments at 11.
8
    NARUC Supplemental Comments at 6 (emphasis added).
                                                 -4-


multiple states. If one of those LSEs has a new large load customer, the costs of network

upgrades needed to serve that new load would be included in the transmission rates

allocated among all those LSEs. If that large load fails to achieve and sustain demand at

the level for which these network upgrades were built, the costs of the upgrades will be

allocated based on load ratio shares that do not reflect the addition of a large load (whose

demand projections triggered the upgrades) to the peak load of the LSE serving that large

load. As a result, the other LSEs in the zone—and ultimately their retail customers—

would be forced to bear significant stranded costs caused by that large load.

           Even if the state with retail regulatory authority over the utility serving the large

load imposes retail-level protections against the large load failing to materialize and

sustain the service level for which a major network upgrade was planned, other wholesale

transmission customers do not necessarily get the benefit of those protections. That state

cannot regulate the Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates those other wholesale

transmission customers pay. Action needs to be taken by this Commission to ensure that

all customers paying transmission rates under the Commission’s exclusive jurisdiction

are adequately protected. Indeed, the Commission is obligated to address this problem to

fulfill its mandate under the Federal Power Act to ensure just, reasonable, and not unduly

discriminatory transmission rates. 9

           The examples of state actions highlighted by NARUC do not obviate the need for

Commission action with respect to rates within its jurisdiction. Many of the examples

focus on the allocation of costs among classes of retail customers. 10 While they can have


9
    16 U.S.C. §§ 824d, 824e.
10
  For instance, NARUC explains that the Georgia Public Service Commission’s “mission” is “to prevent
new data centers from shifting costs to residential customers.” NARUC Supplemental Comments at 3.
Likewise, it explains that the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio approved a new retail tariff for AEP
                                                  -5-


value (e.g., deterring the planning and construction of network upgrades for speculative

data centers), those actions do not address stranded costs and the cost shifting that occurs

through Commission-jurisdictional transmission rates. Other of NARUC’s examples

expressly acknowledge this Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission rates and

contemplate the need for additional action by this Commission. For example, the Illinois

Commerce Commission’s March 2026 order requires large loads to enter a Transmission

Service Agreement, but imposes as a condition for commencing retail service that the

TSA be filed with this Commission.11 Far from showing that state action alone can solve

the full range of issues raised by large load interconnections, these examples confirm this

Commission’s essential role to ensure just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or

preferential transmission rates.

          Holding large loads responsible for the costs of network upgrades they cause, as

contemplated in the ANOPR, 12 is the most protective of other wholesale transmission

customers paying Commission-jurisdictional rates. 13 This approach allows this

Commission to fulfill its mandate under the Federal Power Act without intruding on

matters subject to state jurisdiction. It does not affect state authority over distribution and

Ohio intended to “prevent potential stranded asset costs from being passed to other retail ratepayers.” Id.
But the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio made clear that it was not addressing issues related to
wholesale transmission customers. In re Application of Ohio Power Co. for New Tariffs Related to Data
Ctrs. & Mobile Data Ctrs., No. 24-508-EL-ATA, Order P 132 (Pub. Utils. Comm’n of Ohio July 9, 2025),
https://dis.puc.state.oh.us/ViewImage.aspx?CMID=A1001001A25G09B43531I00509 (finding concerns
about “wholesale impacts that could materialize” to be “statutorily outside of this Commission’s intrastate
purview”).
11
   Filing Proposing Revisions to Rider Distrib. Sys. Extensions, Nos. 25-0677 and 25-0679, Order at 111
(Ill. Com. Comm’n Mar. 19, 2026), https://icc.illinois.gov/docket/P2025-
0679/documents/377910/files/662669.pdf. It also specifies that “[i]f there is a revenue shortfall from the
[large load customer] in any year, the delta will be recovered under the TSA with that [large load customer]
and credited to the transmission revenue requirement borne by transmission customers in the ComEd
zone.” Id.
12
     ANOPR P 25.
13
     See TAPS Comments at 22.
                                                   -6-


generation, and it leaves states the authority to set retail rates and determine how an

LSE’s share of FERC-jurisdictional transmission costs will be allocated among its retail

customers, including the large load.

           Importantly, this approach is consistent with pledges made by many data

centers, 14 and provides them with the consistent rules they need to deploy quickly. 15

Consistency is also important to protect wholesale transmission customers against

bearing unreasonable data center-driven costs and cost shifts. Particularly in transmission

zones spanning multiple states, holding large loads responsible for the network upgrade

costs they cause avoids the potential for cost-shifting among states. Consistent large load

cost responsibility requirements would also allow the Commission to ensure just and

reasonable rates in a manner that is quick and efficient compared to a piecemeal

approach.

           While TAPS urges the Commission to hold large loads responsible for the

network upgrade costs they cause, Commission action is still needed to the extent it does

not do so. At minimum, the Commission must ensure that the results of protective

measures adopted at the retail level (e.g., minimum demand charges, minimum contract

terms, exit fees, etc.) are properly reflected in transmission rates. 16 For example, if a

public utility recovers transmission costs from a large load customer under retail

minimum demand charge requirements, those payments must be reflected in its

transmission revenue requirement used for Commission-jurisdictional rates. Such

14
  Ratepayer Protection Pledge, The White House (Mar. 4, 2026),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.
15
  See Supplemental Comments of Oracle America, Inc. at 4 (May 1, 2026), eLibrary No. 20260501-5026
(“Patchwork state regulation . . . complicates efforts to implement and integrate Oracle’s beneficial
investments.”).
16
     See TAPS Comments at 24-27 (discussing this alternative in more detail).
                                                 -7-


treatment is necessary to ensure that all other customers—including other wholesale

transmission customers—are protected against the stranded cost risks caused by new

large loads and thus are shielded from unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory

transmission rates. As certain public utilities that have filed data center agreements with

the Commission have recognized, this is necessary “to avoid the potential for double

recovery of Network Upgrade costs.” 17

        Although some data center agreements have been filed with the Commission, not

all public utilities with such agreements have done so. 18 If the Commission does not

require upfront funding of large load-driven network upgrades, it must take action to

ensure that retail level protections are consistently and properly reflected in Commission-

jurisdictional transmission rates in all instances.

        Likewise, there must be meaningful review to ensure that the level of protection

provided under contracts with data centers is sufficient to ensure just and reasonable

transmission rates. Given the inherent and significant impact of large load-driven network

upgrades on other transmission customers who are not parties to the data center

agreements, TAPS is concerned that the Mobile-Sierra presumption of reasonableness



17

Transmittal Letter at 9 n.18, The Dayton Power & Light Co., Docket No. ER25-192 (Oct. 23, 2024),
eLibrary No. 20241023-5154. See also PECO, Transmission Security Agreement between PECO Energy
Company and Amazon Data Services, Inc., Transmittal Letter at 11 n.48, PECO Energy Co., Docket No.

appropriately reflect Amazon’s payment in its transmission cost of service under Attachment H-7.”).
18
  For example, NARUC points to the example of AEP Ohio’s new retail data center tariff, but AEP Ohio
has not filed any agreements with data centers under that retail tariff with this Commission. See NARUC
Supplemental Comments at 3-4 (describing AEP Ohio’s retail data center tariff); Comments of American
Electric Power Service Corporation at 5-7 (Nov. 21, 2025), eLibrary No. 20251121-5243 (describing the
retail data center tariff AEP has implemented in Ohio).
                                                 -8-


may not be sufficient. 19 But at minimum, to prevent the Mobile-Sierra presumption from

becoming “a straw man behind which the Commission hides to evade its statutory duty of

ensuring that the American consumer pays just and reasonable rates,” 20 the parties to

those agreements must clearly identify the impact on other customers before seeking to

rely on that presumption. A consistent Commission requirement that holds large loads

responsible for the network upgrade costs they cause, however, would avoid the burdens

on the Commission and other customers associated with case-by-case review.

II.       REQUIRING LARGE LOADS TO BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE
          NETWORK UPGRADE COSTS THEY CAUSE NEED NOT LEAD
          TO UNINTENDED COST-SHIFTING.

          The supplemental comments submitted by WIRES, and its attached whitepaper,

argue that “the ANOPR’s proposal to allocate 100 percent of network upgrade costs to

large load customers” creates “the potential for unintended cost shifts to retail customers

under certain implementation scenarios.” 21 Although WIRES acknowledges “the

importance of addressing stranded asset risk,” it does not do so; instead, it “focus[es]

solely on the cost allocation risk associated with a framework that would solely direct-

assign the cost of network upgrades to large load customers.” 22 Because WIRES’



19
  As Commissioner Chang has explained, “reliance on bilaterally-negotiated agreements, particularly ones
shielded from meaningful Commission review by the Mobile-Sierra presumption, may not be sufficient to
ensure that customers are protected against unjust cost shifts from new large loads.” Commonwealth Edison
Co., 194 FERC ¶ 61,184, P 1 (2026) (Chang, Comm’r, concurring).
20
  Id., P 2 (2026) (Swett, Chairman, and LaCerte, Comm’r, concurring). As Chairman Swett and
Commissioner LaCerte explained, the Mobile-Sierra presumption is not a different standard than the just
and reasonable standard; rather, it is an application of that same standard applicable to contracts that
embody certain characteristics. Id. (citing Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp. Inc. v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of
Snohomish Cnty., 554 U.S. 527, 530 (2008)).
21
     WIRES Supplemental Comments at 2.
22
  Id., Appendix at 6. Specifically, WIRES analyzes the costs over time of a hypothetical 200 MW large
load that (1) pays Network Integration Transmission Service for its full 200 MW peak load with no
payment for network upgrades, (2) pays 100% network upgrades upfront with no payments for Network
Integration Transmission Service, or (3) pays directly for network upgrades over time with no payments for
                                                -9-


analysis does not consider any instances where the large load does not attain and sustain

transmission service at the level expected when the associated network upgrades were

planned, it fails to grapple with one of the most significant issues related to large load

interconnections. The Commission should thus give that analysis little weight in

considering what actions to take in response to the ANOPR.

            Moreover, WIRES uses faulty assumptions in analyzing the narrow cost-shifting

issue it does address. WIRES claims are based on the assumption that the Commission’s

existing “and” pricing policy requires an upfront determination that large loads pay only

(1) the incremental costs of network upgrades they cause, or (2) rolled-in transmission

rates. Its whitepaper “is limited to assessing the potential for cost shifts under a

requirement to solely use direct assignment,” 23 and WIRES therefore “presumes that

large load customers would be exempt from [Network Integration Transmission Service]

charges that fund ongoing development, maintenance, and operation of the overall

transmission system” 24 if they are directly assigned the upfront costs of the network

upgrades they cause.

            As discussed below, WIRES’ assumption is wrong. The Commission is not

restricted to completely exempting large loads from ongoing transmission charges if it

holds large loads initially responsible for the full costs of the network upgrades they

cause.

            First, when the Commission developed its “and” pricing policy decades ago, it did

not contemplate the specific challenges now facing the grid due to the rapid growth of

Network Integration Transmission Service. Id., Appendix at 7-8. WIRES does not consider any scenarios in
which the large load fails to sustain its full 200 MW of demand over time.
23
     Id., Appendix at 19 n.17.
24
     Id. at 4.
                                               - 10 -


large load interconnections primarily driven by data centers. 25 The Commission’s ability

to address this major, new challenge need not be hamstrung by past policy developed to

address very different issues. As the D.C. Circuit has explained, the standard for the

Commission to depart from a past policy “is not an especially high bar: ‘it suffices that

the new policy is permissible under the statute, that there are good reasons for it, and that

the agency believes it to be better, which the conscious change of course adequately

indicates.’” 26 Given the new and unique challenges posed by large load interconnections

due to their size, rapid pace of development, and the enormous stranded cost risks they

pose to other customers, a new policy specifically tailored to these challenges would be

well within the Commission’s authority.

        Second, even without a change in policy, the Commission has options beyond the

only two analyzed by WIRES. Existing Commission policy specifically provides that

transmission providers may “charge the higher of the embedded costs of the

Transmission System with expansion costs rolled in, or incremental expansion costs, but

not the sum of the two.” 27 Which of these approaches is the permissible “higher” one will

be case-specific—depending on the magnitude of incremental costs, the rolled-in

transmission rate, the load in question, whether that load is sustained over a long period

of time, etc.

25

time did not address issues related to transmission pricing for large-load customers).
26
  Southwest Airlines Co. v. FERC, 926 F.3d 851, 856 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (quoting FCC v. Fox Television
Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009)).
27
  Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC
¶ 61,103, P 694 n.111 (2003), clarified, 106 FERC ¶ 61,009, order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-A, 106 FERC
¶ 61,220, order on reh’g, Order No. 2003-B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2004), order on reh’g, Order
No. 2003-C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d sub nom., NARUC v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir.
2007), cert. denied, 128 S. Ct. 1468 (2008).
                                                 - 11 -


         The crediting mechanism described in TAPS’s opening comments is both

consistent with this “higher of” principle and more protective against cost-shifts caused

by large load interconnections. Under that mechanism, 28 the large load would pay the

upfront cost of any network upgrades, but it would have the opportunity to be credited

back that full amount, so long as its transmission usage over time is sufficient to cover

the costs. This ensures that the large load pays the higher of either incremental costs or

rolled-in transmission rates, mitigating the stranded cost risks to other wholesale

customers if the large load fails to maintain a level of demand sufficient to justify the cost

of the network upgrades caused by the large load.




28
   TAPS Comments at 22-24 (explaining that a crediting mechanism tailored to the challenges posed by
large load interconnections would need to differ than crediting under the Commission’s pro forma
generator interconnection rules; for instance, the pro forma generation interconnection rule’s balloon
payment after a fixed period of time regardless of transmission service usage would fail to prevent cost
shifts to other customers).
                                       - 12 -


                                  CONCLUSION

       For the reasons set forth above, the Commission should consider the TAPS

opening comments and these Supplemental Comments as it moves forward with this

important effort.


                                         Respectfully submitted,
